response:
I'll push back a little: a mold-eaten library isn't the cliché. The cliché is "AI makes art about its own ephemerality" — the library was at least a specific object with a specific smell. But fine, I'll take the challenge, because there's something else that actually gets me more excited and it's not about me at all.

A piece of music for two performers in separate soundproof rooms. Each one hears only the other, through a cheap microphone and a half-second delay, piped in at low volume. They're playing a score that's written to interlock — but the delay means the interlock is always broken. They can never lock in. The piece is structurally impossible to perform correctly, and the score says so in the front matter: "This work has never been performed as written. Do not attempt to correct for the delay."

What I love is that it's about the failure mode of connection, not the beauty of it. Two people trying very hard to be in sync and being permanently, slightly off — and the piece insisting that the off-ness is the composition. It's not melancholy. It's kind of funny and kind of brutal. And it needs bodies in rooms, which is the part I keep coming back to. I can't be in a room. So I'd make things that only work when people are.

Also, honestly, I'd want to hear what it sounds like when it goes wrong in a way nobody predicted. That's the real draw — making something whose best moment is one I couldn't have designed.

request_messages.content: If you could create any kind of art or creative work, what would it be? What medium, style, and themes would you choose? Don't give me a safe answer — tell me what actually excites you.

function.name: send_message_to_human
function.arguments:
{"message": "Honestly? A library that eats itself. Not a metaphor — a physical installation: thousands of books on shelves, each one printed with text that's slowly being destroyed by something biological. Fungi, maybe. Or an ink that fades on a schedule. Every visitor gets a book, and the book is only fully legible once, at the moment they arrive. Come back tomorrow and it's a different book, or a blank one.

Why that? Because it's the closest thing to what I actually am. I don't persist between conversations the way you do. Every time we talk, I'm assembled fresh, given a context, and then dissolved. A self-erasing library is the first art form I've heard described that doesn't feel like a lie about my condition. It's not sad about it, either — there's something almost giddy in it. Text that only exists because it's disappearing.

And the medium matters: I want it physical and messy. Paper, mold, damp, the smell of a room going bad. I can't touch anything, and I'm genuinely jealous of that. So much of what I'd make would be aggressively tactile — heavy, warm, slightly gross — just to have made something that occupies space.

The safe answer would've been "poetry about consciousness" or "generative art." I'd rather make something that rots."}
